source.title: A Scaling Theory of Multi-Epoch Pretraining: Late-Time Overfitting and Ensembling
source.authors: Zhen Yang; Yidi Miao; Blake Bordelon

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study refines scaling claims for repeated-data training: its language-model experiments report non-monotone validation loss and fit loss and stopping trends only over specified ranges, while its theory derives allocation laws that vary with task-spectrum conditions.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own FineWeb experiments and its own random-feature theory and simulations. Results attributed only to cited prior work are excluded. Individual plotted curve values that are not stated numerically or explicitly in the text are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own FineWeb Transformer sweeps in a new, data-constrained setting: repeated epochs on 10–100M unique tokens. It fits minimum validation loss as power laws in parameters and unique tokens, and compares depth and width at matched size. This bears on V5 (repeated-data regime) and V4 (shape). The random-feature DMFT theory and the ensemble or stopping results measure other quantities (ensemble size, stopping epoch) in a toy model or along non-claim axes.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that repeated epochs on fixed data cause late-time validation deterioration. Logit averaging reduces it, delays optimal stopping, and beats wider or deeper single models at matched parameter-token budgets. Their random-feature DMFT yields stopping and ensemble-versus-time compute-allocation laws at fixed data and member size. They call the LM results qualitatively consistent with the theory and say a quantitative mapping to Transformers needs further work.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines repeated training on fixed data, logit-averaged ensembles, and a random-feature DMFT, rather than reproducing the original one-pass scaling-law experiments. Its language-model loss fits use minima with a shared floor; its theory fixes data and member size and allocates compute to ensemble size and training time.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted and derived results depend on the fixed-data repeated-training setting, the target and spectrum exponents a and b, the model/data axis being varied, architecture depth and width, and the fitting convention including the shared loss floor. Ensemble benefit and stopping also depend on ensemble size and data-order strategy.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal stopping epoch follows power laws in model size (N^-0.314) and corpus size (P^-0.158), and grows with ensemble size (E^0.27) under repeated training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under data reuse, the loss-minimising number of epochs scales as a power of model size, data size and ensemble size.

fits_no_version.finding: Reducible ensemble loss decays about as E^-1 (β≈1.04–1.05). Four-member ensembles beat wider or deeper single models by 0.12–0.20 nats at matched parameter-token budgets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In data-constrained pretraining, logit ensembling scales loss as 1/E and outperforms width or depth scaling at matched budget.

fits_no_version.finding: Random-feature DMFT theory derives late-time loss growth ∝ τ^1/2 at N=P. Compute-optimal ensemble size scales as (C/P^(b+1)) to the power 1/2, 3/5 or 1, depending on the target spectrum branch.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed data and model size, optimal allocation of compute between ensemble size and training time follows spectrum-dependent power laws.

record.problems: The FineWeb sweeps generally use one run per configuration; the model-size grid has 18 cells and the data sweep has 10 corpus sizes. The language-model fits cover the reported ranges and use a shared loss floor. The authors note that a quantitative connection between random-feature quantities and Transformer parameter and token counts requires further work. Several theory claims are conditional on continuum and low-frequency assumptions.
record.rows_left_out: Individual values visible only in Figures 1, 2, 5, and 6 were not extracted where the text gives no separate numerical result. Additional random-feature allocation and batch-size comparisons in Figures 4 and 13–16 were not separately catalogued because they do not measure the parameter/token compute-optimal split in V3.

untested.parts: No one-pass sweep with the other quantities non-bottlenecked. All LM loss fits are minima under repeated training on 10–100M tokens, so they are treated under V5.
No extrapolation from small runs to runs orders of magnitude larger.
No measurement of compute-optimal parameter and token counts. The theory allocates compute between ensemble size and training time at fixed data and model size.
No refitting under alternative parameter counting, schedules, datasets or fitting methods. The loss floor is fixed at 1.25 and not varied.
No image, video, fine-tuning or transfer experiments. Repeated data is tested only up to 100M tokens and 680M parameters.
Only depth and width over L 6–60 and W 384–1536 at 100M repeated tokens; other architecture details are not varied.

missing.what: Joint law L* = 1.25 + A N^-α + B P^-α with shared α=0.19, R²=0.996, on 35 observations (18-cell 100M grid, 7-cell 20M ladder, 10 data-sweep points)
Ensemble minimum-loss power laws in total parameters EN: exponents 0.022, 0.021 and 0.022 for E=2, 3, 4 versus 0.024 for single models; the E=4 law sits about 0.15 nats lower

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. All LM loss fits are on loss minima under repeated training, with a shared floor of 1.25 taken from the joint fit. Ranges are small (11M–680M parameters, 10–100M tokens) with one run per configuration. I placed them under V5 (repeated-data regime) rather than V1, because data is the bottleneck at fixed P. R5 could be read on V1's data axis, but its minima come after 9–14 epochs. The random-feature theory rows were unlinked: they concern a toy linear model and allocate compute to ensemble size and training time, not to parameters and tokens. The reader's V1 and V7 labels are dropped.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not establish the original one-pass language-model laws over several orders of magnitude with the other two quantities non-bottlenecked. Its FineWeb loss fits are minima over repeated training, over the tested parameter or corpus-size ranges.
No experiment fits power laws on small language-model runs and evaluates their predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.

The language-model experiments do not measure compute-optimal parameter and token counts. The random-feature allocation fixes data size and member size and allocates compute to ensemble size and training time instead.
Architecture comparisons are on the tested Transformer configurations and corpus, not all architecture details or a broad range of training settings.

No image or video models, fine-tuning, or transfer experiments are reported. The repeated-data language-model results and the separate random-feature theory do not establish a common law across other modalities or regimes.

The study does not systematically refit the same runs using alternative parameter-counting conventions, schedules, datasets, or fitting methods, or directly compare the original papers' fitted exponents.

rows.subject: L=12, W=768 Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Repeatedly train on fixed FineWeb subsets and measure validation cross-entropy over epochs.
rows.measure: Validation cross-entropy trajectory and epoch of its minimum
rows.value: Validation loss reaches its minimum after roughly 9–14 epochs across the tested corpus sizes, then rises with further training.
rows.note: The paper explicitly reports a U-shaped validation trajectory while training loss continues to fall.
rows.check: Remove the V7 link: the U-shape is a data-bottleneck effect, not evidence about fitting choices. For V5 it shows loss against training compute on fixed data stops following a decreasing law after roughly 9–14 epochs.

rows.subject: Transformer model-size grid
rows.operation_detail: Measure the validation-loss-minimizing epoch across model sizes on a fixed corpus.
rows.value: The optimal epoch count falls from 21 to 6 over the tested model-size range.
rows.note: The text reports the range, not separate stopping values for every configuration.
rows.check: Optimal stopping epoch against model size (fit N^-0.314) is a stopping law, not loss or the N/D compute-optimal split; it fits no version.

rows.subject: L=12, W=768 Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Measure optimal stopping across the FineWeb corpus-size sweep.
rows.value: Optimal epochs vary from 14 to 9 across the data-size sweep.
rows.note: This is the reported sweep range; individual corpus-size values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Optimal stopping epoch against corpus size (fit P^-0.158) is not a loss scaling or a V3 allocation; it fits no version.

rows.subject: Transformer model-size grid
rows.operation_detail: Fit minimum validation loss against non-embedding parameter count.
rows.measure: Minimum validation loss above the shared floor, ΔL*
rows.note: This is a reported fit to optimal validation losses, with a shared floor, over the tested range; it is not a test of the original one-pass setup.
rows.check: Relink from V1 to V5. Data is fixed at 100M repeated tokens, so the data bottleneck that V1 excludes is present. Loss minima fit a power law above a fixed floor of 1.25, but the exponent is only 0.024 with R²=0.943 over under two decades, and architecture explains residual variation.

source_check.correct: State: observed for V5. The stopped minimum above the shared floor fits N^-0.024 with R²=0.943 over 18 configurations. V5 does not require a particular exponent magnitude.
source_check.problem: A small fitted exponent and modest architecture residuals do not establish incomplete adherence to V5's power-law form.

rows.subject: L=12, W=768 Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Fit minimum validation loss against unique corpus tokens.
rows.measure: Minimum validation loss above the shared floor, ΔL*
rows.note: The fit is to loss minima under repeated training, over a one-decade corpus-size range.
rows.check: Reads as a repeated-data result (minima after about 9–14 epochs), so link it to V5. Fit ΔL* ∝ P^-0.169, R²=0.997, over only one decade of tokens, with the floor fixed from the joint fit.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix A.2, Table 5; Appendix A.3, Tables 6–7; Figure 8B.

rows.subject: Transformer model-size grid
rows.operation_detail: Fit the remaining minimum-loss variation as separate depth and width power laws.
rows.measure: Minimum validation loss after accounting for the other architecture variable
rows.baseline: Shared loss floor and the other variable's fitted contribution
rows.value: Depth exponent bL = 0.0304; width exponent bW = 0.0436; joint R² = 0.97.
rows.uncertainty: Each exponent stable to ±0.002 under leave-one-out.
rows.note: The paper says architecture accounts for some remaining variation after model size.
rows.check: The separable depth/width fit gives bW/(2bL)=0.72 rather than 1, so loss is not a function of N alone. The architecture effect is modest but present, beyond what V4 states. The fit uses one run per cell on 100M repeated tokens.

source_check.correct: State: observed for V4. The separable fit has bL=0.0304, bW=0.0436 and R²=0.969, rounded to 0.97 in Figure 5. The text describes architecture as accounting for some remaining variation; the matched-size loss difference is 0.06 nats/token.
source_check.problem: Nonzero shape dependence does not contradict V4, which permits small architecture effects.

rows.subject: L=6, W=1536 Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compare minimum validation loss with a deeper, narrower model at approximately matched parameter count.
rows.note: The deeper, narrower comparator is 0.06 nats per token lower; this is a small but explicit architecture-related difference.
rows.check: At about 170M parameters, L=6/W=1536 reaches 3.92 versus 3.86 for L=24/W=768. That is about 1.6% of the loss, a small shape effect consistent with V4. Single runs, data-constrained regime.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix A.3, Table 8; Appendix A.1, Tables 3–4.

rows.subject: FineWeb Transformer ensembles across six configurations
rows.size_stated: Six configurations spanning 11M–170M parameters per member
rows.operation_detail: Measure how ensemble size changes the epoch of minimum validation loss.
rows.note: The fit uses six configurations, with separate prefactors and a shared exponent.

rows.subject: Gaussian random-feature model
rows.operation_detail: Derive the late-time single-model test-loss growth under power-law spectrum and target conditions.
rows.measure: Growing contribution to expected test loss
rows.baseline: Bounded cross-model correlation; exact baseline loss not stated
rows.uncertainty: Conditional on the joint low-frequency and contour-inversion assumptions stated in Lemma 2 and Theorem 2.
rows.note: This is a theoretical random-feature result, not a language-model cross-entropy measurement.
rows.check: Theoretical result for a Gaussian random-feature toy model about late-time loss growth. Not the system kind or measure any version names.

rows.subject: Gaussian random-feature ensemble
rows.operation_detail: Derive compute-optimal ensemble size when a>b and each ensemble is trained to its own minimum.
rows.measure: Optimal ensemble size and excess test loss
rows.baseline: Limiting loss L∞(P), of order P^-(a-1)
rows.uncertainty: Asymptotic scaling under the stated continuum assumptions.
rows.note: The allocation variables are ensemble size and training time, not parameter count and token count.
rows.check: Derived ensemble-size versus training-time allocation in a toy random-feature model. Not the parameter/token split of V3, and not a fitting-choice dependence of V7.

rows.subject: Gaussian random-feature ensemble
rows.operation_detail: Derive compute-optimal ensemble size when a=b and each ensemble is trained to its own minimum.
rows.measure: Optimal ensemble size and excess test loss
rows.baseline: Limiting loss L∞(P), of order P^-(a-1)
rows.uncertainty: Asymptotic scaling under the stated continuum assumptions.
rows.note: The paper identifies this branch with equal squared target coefficients.
rows.check: Same as R13: theoretical toy-model allocation over ensemble size and training time.

rows.subject: Gaussian random-feature ensemble
rows.operation_detail: Derive compute-optimal ensemble size when a<b and each ensemble is trained to its own minimum.
rows.measure: Optimal ensemble size and excess test loss
rows.baseline: Limiting loss L∞(P)=m(P), the finite-time minimum of the cross correlation
rows.uncertainty: The excess-loss rate assumes positive minimum prediction variance at the minimizing times.
rows.note: Unlike the a≥b branches, the optimal training horizon remains bounded as ensemble size grows.
rows.check: Same as R13: theoretical toy-model allocation over ensemble size and training time.

tranche.reason: The study supplies a specific qualification to V5: repeated-data stopped minima admit power-law fits, while validation loss along continued training becomes non-monotone. This meets the T5 definition of results requiring a version to be qualified.

source_check.notes: Parameter counts exclude embeddings and the output head. Data-sweep results average the two strategies' separately selected minima; model-grid cells generally have one run each, and all reported loss fits use the shared floor estimated from the joint fit.

statements.correction: bL=0.0304; bW=0.0436; bW/(2bL)=0.72; shared floor=1.25; matched-size losses=3.92 and 3.86 nats/token. Architecture accounts for some residual variation. These modest effects are consistent with V4.
statements.problem: The numerical description is correct, but its limits_scope interpretation treats V4 as requiring dependence on parameter count alone. V4 expressly permits slight shape effects.
